articles.title: A Blockbuster Devin Booker Trade Idea That Actually Makes Sense
articles.summary: The 2025-26 Phoenix Suns returned to respectability with 45 wins, fighting through two play-in games before falling to the Oklahoma City Thunder in a quick sweep. Through 10 games this season, the Suns (4-6) have yet to click, as the competition in the Western Conference is unforgiving.
articles.body:
The 2025-26 Phoenix Suns returned to respectability with 45 wins, fighting through two play-in games before falling to the Oklahoma City Thunder in a quick sweep. Through 10 games this season, the Suns (4-6) have yet to click, as the competition in the Western Conference is unforgiving.

Unless the Suns can fix their porous defense and start racking up wins, it may be time for the franchise to explore trading five-time All-Star Devin Booker. Now in his 12th season, Booker remains a prolific 25.1-point scorer, but he's carrying a sizable four-year, $252.6 million contract (with a player option before the 2029-30 season).

The Atlanta Hawks stand out as a viable partner in this theoretical trade concept.

The Phoenix Suns receive: CJ McCollum, Kingston Flemings, Dorian Finney-Smith, Corey Kispert, protected 2028 first-rounder

Phoenix added two years to Booker's deal in July 2025, rewarding its best player with another projected $134.5 million—the exact figure won't be decided until the 2028-29 salary cap is set. The franchise may not regret the loyalty; it may just find its way out of paying for it.

The Suns would seek a greater pick haul than the one included in this deal, which would be top-5 protected for three years before converting into a pair of second-rounders (New York Knicks in 2030, Sacramento Kings in 2033). The two teams can hammer out those details. Phoenix's challenge is the heft of Booker's deal, a number large enough to turn off most potential suitors.

The key player coming back from the Hawks is Flemings, their No. 8 overall selection in June. The 6'3" 19-year-old would fill the significant point-guard vacancy on the Suns. He's a willing defender and is already productive, averaging 8.5 points and 4.4 assists in 21.9 minutes per game. Flemings doesn't shoot the three often (1.9 attempts) but has converted 42.9 percent through his first 11 games.

The pivot away from Booker doesn't represent tanking, with veteran scorer McCollum taking his place. McCollum also brings point-guard skills to Phoenix. Kispert isn't a regular part of Atlanta's rotation, but he's a capable wing shooter.

The Suns would need to waive or trade a couple of players to open roster space for the deal, possibly Jamaree Bouyea and Rasheer Fleming. A trade exception generated for Booker is negligible at under $600,000.

The Hawks returned to the postseason after a two-year absence, tied with the Toronto Raptors for the fifth-best record in the Eastern Conference (46-36). After taking a surprising 2-1 lead over the New York Knicks, the Hawks dropped the next three to the eventual champions.

The team is off to a strong start this year, too, with its egalitarian style of play. Power forward Jalen Johnson leads Atlanta in assists at 7.2 per game. Nickeil Alexander-Walker leads the team in scoring at 21.9 points per game. The combination should work for the regular season, but Booker ups the stakes.

When Atlanta needed a big bucket against the Knicks, McCollum was the go-to playoff shotmaker. Booker, 30, is five years younger and is presently a more reliable scorer. The trio of Johnson, Alexander-Walker, and Booker would be difficult for any postseason opponent. With the defense of Dyson Daniels and Lu Dort, Onyeka Okongwu at center, plus Aaron Wiggins and Jock Landale off the bench, the Hawks would be an interesting contender in the East.

Atlanta might be willing to trade more draft capital to keep Flemings out of the deal, but that would mean a luxury-tax bill for a franchise that historically minds its spending. Subbing in Wiggins could be a viable alternative for the Hawks. Including Landale is another path, though that would thin out a center rotation that already needs help.

Another possibility is a big on the buyout market, though the Hawks may need to wait to execute this deal with the Suns until the Feb. 11 trade deadline, pausing to fill their 13th and 14th roster spots for a couple of weeks to avoid the tax.

Email Eric Pincus at eric.pincus@gmail.com and follow him on X @EricPincus .

articles.title: Can the NBA Do Anything About Its Growing Injury Problem?
articles.summary: On Thursday, the Golden State Warriors (and really, anyone who enjoys watching good basketball) got some tough news.
articles.body:
On Thursday, the Golden State Warriors (and really, anyone who enjoys watching good basketball) got some tough news.

ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Stephen Curry will miss at least the next two weeks with "an oblique abdominal tear."

With yet another high-profile star going down, it's time to ask whether this injury problem is a growing trend or just a well-reported one, and whether the NBA, its teams, or its stars can do anything about it.

For those who haven't been keeping track at home, since the regular season tipped off on October 20, we've now lost the following (with their original injury timelines):

Paolo Banchero (4-to-6 weeks with a high ankle sprain)

Jalen Suggs (at least two weeks with a bone bruise on his knee)

Jalen Williams (potentially the entire season with a dislocated left ankle and fractured fibula)

Cason Wallace (potentially the entire season with a torn labrum)

Kawhi Leonard (multiple weeks with swelling in his knee)

Jaren Jackson Jr. (6-to-8 weeks with a torn MCL)

Anthony Edwards (up to two months following an arthroscopic procedure on his knee)

Tyrese Haliburton (at least two weeks with a hamstring strain)

Ja Morant (at least four weeks with a hamstring strain)

Chet Holmgren (8-to-10 weeks with a small patellar tendon tear)

Lauri Markkanen (at least one month with a non-displaced fracture in his hand)

Caleb Wilson (4-to-6 weeks with a fractured hand)

Stephen Curry (with the aforementioned oblique injury)

Beyond that, Shaedon Sharpe, Kon Knueppel, AJ Dybantsa, Jimmy Butler, Bradley Beal, Grant Williams and Nic Claxton all carried injuries into this season.

And we've also seen an alarming increase in Achilles tears in recent years. In just the last three seasons (including 2026-27), that injury has claimed DaRon Holmes, James Wiseman, Isaiah Jackson, Dru Smith, Dejounte Murray, Damian Lillard, Jayson Tatum, Haliburton, Donte DiVincenzo, Ariel Hukporti and Ben Simmons.

And to get one of the questions asked earlier out of the way right now, it doesn't look like this is something that just feels like a problem because of the way the NBA is currently covered.

Dr. Brian Sutterer, a sports medicine doctor with a large social media following, posted recent findings showing that injury absences per rotation player are much higher than they were 20 years ago. Serious injuries (like an Achilles tear) are also more common.

The general refrain, at least among many sports media personalities, is that the season is too long.

At the pace the game is played now, players' bodies simply can't take the rigors of an 82-game campaign. Everyone is too explosive now. They have to cover much more ground on defense because offenses are so spaced out . In a word, the game is just more demanding than it was in previous eras, to the point that it's time to reduce the schedule.

The catch is that the logic and potential outcomes have real problems.

For one thing, the injuries piling up now are happening in October and November. The season is less than a month old. Even with a hypothetical 65-game schedule (or whatever other number might be popular), these injuries would still be happening.

The retort may be that the current avalanche is a byproduct of wear and tear from previous years, but Banchero, Suggs and Morant, just to name a few, aren't coming off deep playoff runs.

What's more, team training and medical staff have effectively already shortened individual players' seasons. "Load management" is a concept that has been popularized during the 20-year sample Sutterer examined.

Players get more off-nights from games and practices than in earlier eras, but the frequency of injuries hasn't gone down.

Beyond shortening the season, some want to shorten games from 48 to 40 minutes.

The problems here are even easier to spot.

For one, it could all but eliminate role players. Some teams would still play their starters 30-35 minutes, leaving little time for reserves and the strategies involved in using them.

That said, if shortening games did cause stars to drop below 30 minutes per game, it would also mess with individual players' legacies.

In baseball and football, totals for home runs, touchdowns or other numbers are tracked almost religiously. In basketball, for about as long as it's been an organized sport, the measuring stick of choice is most commonly "per game" averages.

MVP numbers from a winner playing 28 minutes per game, rather than 36, would look odd compared to historical peers. Because while we have easier access to "per-minute" or (preferably) "per-possession" numbers today, viewers are raised and trained on points, rebounds and assists per game.

On top of all of the above, money could stand in the way. For the league, any reduction in inventory (whether through fewer games or fewer minutes) likely means lower revenue, at least in the short term.

Some could argue that scarcity would eventually make the remaining games more valuable.

But if there's one overarching theme of Adam Silver's tenure, it may be that revenue is a tough concern to top.

Ultimately, the best way forward may run counter to popular arguments.

In a recent appearance on Bill Simmons' podcast, longtime coach Doc Rivers suggested that practicing more could actually help. Sutterer shared a similar sentiment on X.

Preparing the body for a more rigorous version of basketball may simply require more rigorous preparation and training. Some (though certainly not all) of the rest may need to be replaced with some form of conditioning, plyometrics or other mobility training.

Surviving an 82-game gauntlet, plus multiple rounds in the playoffs, has always been part of the bargain for winning a championship. No one wants an uptick in injuries. Freak accidents, such as the one that sent Jalen Williams to the injury report, are particularly tough to see.

But the most common response over the years—load management—hasn't worked. It just hasn't.

Maybe it's time to focus less on rest and more on better preparing players' bodies for the demands of today's NBA. More conditioning, more purposeful training and perhaps even more practice.

It's an approach worth exploring before shortening the season, rewriting the record books or fundamentally changing the sport.

It's an option that won't affect the decades-long legacy of the NBA, and it's time to try it.

articles.title: New NBA Power Rankings as Boston Celtics Rise, 76ers Slide, and Injuries Pile Up
articles.summary: Another week of NBA action is done, and the injuries just keep piling up.
articles.body:
Another week of NBA action is done, and the injuries just keep piling up.

The latest additions to the league's growing list of absences are MVP candidate Stephen Curry and Rookie of the Year candidate Caleb Wilson.

At this point, the league looks more like a war of attrition than it maybe ever has. And that will obviously impact this week's rankings.

Of course, that's not the only factor. Based on the criteria that's guided us for years—team and individual numbers, recent performance, championship chances and plenty of subjectivity—this is how the entire league stacks up now.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

The Chicago Bulls aren't just losing games. They're doing it in pretty spectacular fashion.

Less than a month into the season, they already have three losses of at least 30 points. On Wednesday, they led the San Antonio Spurs by 22 in the second quarter, had coughed up that entire lead by the 8:05 mark in the third and wound up losing by five.

Now an eighth of the way through what's shaping up to be an awfully trying campaign, Chicago's top four scorers (Caleb Wilson, Norman Powell, Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey) are shooting a combined 41.7 percent from the field and 31.1 percent from deep.

Some writers (including this one) thought there was enough veteran talent and know-how that came over from the Miami Heat to at least make the Milwaukee Bucks moderately competitive.

Surely, we thought, a team with a perennial 20-point-per-game scorer like Tyler Herro, a well-rounded forward like Jaime Jaquez, a three-and-D center like Myles Turner and an emerging playmaker like Ryan Rollins wouldn't get totally embarrassed every night.

But oh, we were wrong. We were very, very wrong. Herro is scoring alright, but he's clearly part of the problem on defense. Turner looks older, slower and completely checked out.

And though there's at least one bright spot (Brayden Burries' feel for the game and absurd offensive rebounding abilities look legit), Milwaukee looks destined for the relegation zone right now.

It probably doesn't even matter whether the Sacramento Kings can finally find realistic suitors for Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis.

Their presence on the roster clearly isn't leading to wins. And more importantly, it's not getting in the way of Darius Acuff's ascension.

If you carve the first four games of the season off Acuff's averages, the rookie is putting up an eye-popping 28.9 points, 8.7 assists and 3.9 threes, while shooting 39.1 percent from deep.

Outside of him, Kings games are a tough watch. But with each passing week, it looks more and more like Sacramento may have a long-term franchise cornerstone.

Even the biggest skeptics of the Utah Jazz's offseason hype could not have seen this coming.

There was always a chance they weren't going to live up to their new, lofty expectations, but we're nearly a month into this campaign, and Utah has just one win.

If there's a silver lining, it's that another onslaught of injuries has opened up more time and scoring opportunities for the young combo of Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey.

Over their last four games, Peterson is averaging 23.0 points and 4.5 assists while shooting 39.4 percent from deep. Bailey is adding 15.0 points, 1.8 threes, 1.5 steals and 1.3 blocks per game.

The Charlotte Hornets may have expected to take a slight step back this season after trading LaMelo Ball, but they certainly couldn't have anticipated Grayson Allen being their best player.

Thanks in large part to the injuries that have piled up on this roster (Kon Knueppel has played a grand total of one minute, and Brandon Miller is now out too), Allen not only leads the Hornets in 2026-27 wins over replacement player ; he has more (a lot more) than the rest of the roster combined.

There's still a chance everything looks better when Knueppel is back. Another late-season surge isn't impossible. But it wouldn't be at all surprising to learn that some in Charlotte's front office are having some seller's remorse over that LaMelo deal.

At our last check-in with the New Orleans Pelicans, they were .500, coming off a four-game winning streak and rocking a respectable plus-2.3 net rating.

One week, four losses and three blowouts later, the Pelicans are suddenly 25th in net rating and looking dreadful on the defensive end.

If this keeps up much longer, relegation zone or not, New Orleans may need to think about finally ending the Zion Williamson era, trading the vets and throwing as many developmental minutes at Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen as possible.

The Los Angeles Clippers ended their week with a blowout loss to the Phoenix Suns.

And though it's becoming increasingly clear that they need someone (like, oh say, Keaton Wagler) to provide a little playmaking in addition to Darius Garland, they also aren't winning his minutes.

These numbers are still prone to wild, early-season swings, but L.A. is minus-17.3 points per 100 possessions when Garland is on the floor and plus-21.1 when he's off.

Right now, lineups anchored by Brook Lopez and filled out with aggressive defenders are giving the Clippers a much better shot at competitiveness than the ones led by Garland.

This week, the Brooklyn Nets gave us a pretty vivid example of how dramatically things can swing in today's three-point-heavy NBA (especially for a bad team).

Sunday, they lost by 37 to the Dallas Mavericks and shot 11-of-39 from deep. In their very next game, the Nets beat the New Orleans Pelicans by 34 and hit 20 of their 41 three-point attempts.

Sometimes, it really is just a make-or-miss league. And when the Nets can get two or three players to join Michael Porter Jr. in doing some damage from the outside (like Egor Dëmin did on Wednesday, when he hit four threes and scored 22 points), the Nets are close enough to passable on the other end to be competitive.

They came against two of the absolute worst teams in the league (the Sacramento Kings and Utah Jazz), but the Orlando Magic ended their week with back-to-back wins. And Franz Wagner is starting to look more capable of carrying an offense like an alpha.

Over his last three games, Franz is putting up 33.7 points, 7.0 rebounds and 6.3 assists.

And though he won't produce at quite that level when Paolo Banchero comes back, if Wagner can maintain some of the confidence he's building now, the Magic could go on a little run (though Banchero's return is likely still several weeks away).

The Washington Wizards got off to an encouraging start this season. They arrived at last week's version of the power rankings with a positive net rating. And Anthony Davis has generally looked like the younger, healthier version of himself.

But he and Trae Young haven't injected as much winning attitude into the organization as many expected them to.

They put up a spirited effort in Thursday's loss to the Detroit Pistons, but they've now dropped six straight and have their next two contests against above-.500 Western Conference foes.

If they keep losing while Davis keeps producing (he's up to 25.6 points, 10.5 rebounds and 1.0 blocks for the season), expect trade rumors to start swirling around him.

After starting the week 0-2, the Indiana Pacers needed a win on Wednesday. They got it against the Washington Wizards.

And though that wasn't really a juggernaut opponent, that contest may have laid out the blueprint for survival without Tyrese Haliburton (who's still recovering from a hamstring strain).

Andrew Nembhard did his best Haliburton impression, leaned into playmaking more than scoring and kept the bigs involved throughout the night. Nembhard had 10 dimes, while Pascal Siakam (28 points on 17 shots) and Ivica Zubac (20 points on 15 shots) led the team in field-goal attempts.

It was an old-school, guard-sets-up-everyone-else approach that could help Indiana at least stay competitive until Haliburton returns.

It helps that they closed out their week with back-to-back games against the Los Angeles Clippers and Charlotte Hornets, but the Phoenix Suns also beat the Houston Rockets this week.

And their superstar is starting to play like one.

Over his last six appearances (a stretch that includes four Suns wins), Devin Booker is averaging 27.7 points, 4.8 assists and 1.7 steals, while shooting 50.0 percent from the field and 38.6 percent from deep.

The Toronto Raptors are 2-6 in their last eight, and those two wins came against the Los Angeles Clippers and Milwaukee Bucks.

Surprise, surprise. This team is a lot worse when their best player is out. And that means more for the Raptors than it does for most other squads.

Kawhi Leonard's health has been one of the league's biggest red flags for years. Toronto staying close enough to the top of the East to seriously contend will require them to not only win games without Leonard, but to win a lot of them.

This almost certainly won't be his last extended absence, and the Raptors have to win at a higher pace during the next one.

It's taken a while, and there are still some pretty serious concerns about the Giannis Antetokounmpo-led offense (that still ranks in the bottom half of the league), but the Miami Heat are finally getting some traction.

They've won five of their last seven games. Davion Mitchell (16.5 points and 8.5 assists), Klay Thompson (14.4 points) and Pelle Larsson (11.4 points and 3.5 assists) are all averaging double-figures and shooting at least 40 percent from deep.

And when Giannis is on the floor with all three of those shooters, Miami is (small-sample alert!) plus-25.6 points per 100 possessions.

The Golden State Warriors ended their week with a loss, but it was on the road and against the Houston Rockets, who look like a bona fide contender. That's not what could dampen the team or its fans' spirits.

That unfortunate distinction goes to Thursday's news that Stephen Curry suffered an oblique tear and will be reevaluated (though won't necessarily return) in two weeks.

On the season, Curry is averaging 27.8 points and 3.9 assists in just 26.3 minutes. He's a legitimate MVP candidate. And without him, the Warriors' good start could crater.

It doesn't have to, though. Golden State doesn't have to keep winning at its current pace. It can merely survive Curry's absence, thanks in large part to rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, who's putting up 21.7 points, 7.4 rebounds and 3.7 assists, while shooting 42.6 percent from deep.

If he keeps this team afloat for the next month or so, he could have Rookie of the Year wrapped up by December.

The Dallas Mavericks ended their week with a blowout loss to the Anthony Edwards-less Minnesota Timberwolves. And their last three wins came against the Utah Jazz, Brooklyn Nets and Indiana Pacers.

But they also have quality wins over the Houston Rockets, Oklahoma City Thunder and Miami Heat (a team that's slowly rounding into form).

And more importantly, their sophomore sensation is already looking like a soon-to-be-perennial MVP candidate.

The Timberwolves held Cooper Flagg to 12 points on Thursday, but he's averaging 24.6 points, 6.9 rebounds, 6.5 assists and 2.2 steals.

The Atlanta Hawks are off to a solid start in terms of wins and losses.

When Jalen Johnson and Nickeil Alexander-Walker are both on the floor, they're outscoring opponents by 3.5 points per 100 possessions.

Aaron Wiggins (14.9 points) looks like a solid addition. CJ McCollum's willingness to go to the bench looks like a win for the second unit. And Kingston Flemings has shown real upside since moving into the starting five.

But there's still plenty to prove here. All seven of their wins are against below-.500 Eastern Conference teams. And Johnson and Dyson Daniels shooting a combined 18.2 percent from deep is a real concern.

The Memphis Grizzlies' 6-0 start was fun. There's still plenty of reason for long-term optimism. Cameron Boozer already looks like one of the game's better playmaking bigs.

But after losing to the Denver Nuggets in Memphis on Wednesday, the Grizzlies have now dropped four of their last five. And it's becoming increasingly clear that Boozer may be the bellwether of this team.

During the six-game winning streak, he averaged 17.3 points, 10.5 rebounds and 5.7 assists, while shooting 35.9 percent from deep. Since then, he's at 14.2 points, 9.0 rebounds and 5.2 assists, with a 20.0 three-point percentage.

The Cleveland Cavaliers, fresh off their 2026 Eastern Conference Finals appearance, fell below .500 this week.

At least on podcasts and social media timelines, the sky was falling in Cleveland. It was time to somehow break up the Donovan Mitchell-Evan Mobley-Jarrett Allen core. James Harden was washed.

But the Cavs proved on Wednesday that they can still hit a contender-like gear when properly motivated. They beat the New York Knicks (in Madison Square Garden) behind 32 points from Harden. And all four of the above shot at least 50 percent from the field.

One game doesn't suddenly fix this team. There are still concerns about the fit between Harden and Mitchell. There's still an argument to trade one of the bigs. But Wednesday was a good reminder of the ceiling this group can get to on offense.

The Denver Nuggets have scratched and clawed their way to a near-50-win pace through 10 games, but the load being carried by Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray has never looked heavier.

Murray is off to an absurd start, averaging 26.2 points and 5.9 assists, while shooting 51.3 percent from deep. Jokić is way off his typical pace, but he's still adding 23.5 points, 10.8 rebounds and 9.0 assists.

But after that, there may not be a single Nugget who can be counted on for consistent nightly production. And this offseason's big signing, DeMar DeRozan, is shooting 41.0 percent from the field and 14.3 percent from deep, while doing little to change the years-long reality of the dreaded "non-Jokić minutes."

A 39-point win over the Wizards on Saturday did wonders for the Oklahoma City Thunder's season-long net rating, but their injury-induced weaknesses were on display in back-to-back losses to close out the week against the Portland Trail Blazers.

Ajay Mitchell and Jared McCain have done a solid job of filling Jalen Williams' shoes on the offensive end, but there's still more pressure on Shai Gilgeous-Alexander without Williams around.

And more importantly, on the other end, without Williams, Chet Holmgren and Cason Wallace, OKC isn't the turnover-generating machine it typically is.

Starting this coming week with games against the Los Angeles Clippers and Sacramento Kings should get the Thunder back on track, but this version of the team is going to struggle against stiffer competition.

We're roughly a seventh of the way into the Portland Trail Blazers' 2026-27 campaign, and they're still in the top four in the West with a roster that looks brilliantly tailored to the strengths of its top two players.

Deni Avdija and Damian Lillard, first of all, complement each other well. The former's slashing is pulling defenses away from Lillard. Lillard's shooting is making Avdija's driving lanes more accessible.

And all around them, Portland boasts tons of defense, shooting and tenacity.

It'll be hard for anyone to join the tier of MVP candidacy currently occupied by Luka Dončić and Victor Wembanyama, but Cade Cunningham's superstar performance on Thursday should firmly put him in the next one.

In a double-overtime road win over the Washington Wizards, Cade tallied 52 points on 16-of-25 shooting, handed out 11 assists and didn't commit a single turnover.

He was scoring like Luka, while controlling the game like a prime Chris Paul. And while it's fair to point out that the numbers were enhanced by two overtimes and a less-than-stellar Washington defense, it's harder to nitpick in the context of Cade's whole season.

With his running mate, Jalen Duren, missing all but two games this season, Cunningham has carried Detroit to an 8-3 record while averaging 25.0 points, 7.9 assists and 2.0 threes.

The New York Knicks' record is still underwhelming, but it's way too early to press the panic button.

They're still top 10 in the league in both offense and defense. And four of their five losses have come against teams that entered the season considered to be title contenders (or fringe title contenders).

If they have a losing record over their upcoming four-game road trip when they play the Pacers without Haliburton, the Raptors (presumably) without Kawhi (twice) and the Timberwolves without Ant, then we can start to worry.

Their 10-3 record is more important than all the caveats that came with it, but this new title contender showed its vulnerability this week.

The Sixers started this stretch with a 24-point loss to the uninspiring Cleveland Cavaliers. And on Tuesday, they got annihilated by the Boston Celtics in Jaylen Brown's first matchup against Jayson Tatum.

Following the disappointing stretch, Philadelphia's ho-hum net rating now ranks 15th in the league. And Joel Embiid has failed to shoot better than 50 percent from the field in 10 of his 11 appearances.

The Los Angeles Lakers just keep winning. And Luka Dončić just keeps scoring.

Even after a couple "down" games (by his absurd standards), Luka is averaging 38.6 points, 10.8 free-throw attempts, 7.6 assists, 7.5 rebounds and 2.0 steals, while shooting 40.8 percent from deep and 86.6 percent from the line.

And these obviously aren't empty stats. L.A. is first in the West, and its net rating with Dončić on the floor ( plus-19.0 ) is miles better than the one without him (minus-11.8).

The Houston Rockets had a bit of a lull earlier this month, when they lost back-to-back games against the Timberwolves and Suns, but they bounced back with victories over above-.500 Denver and red-hot Golden State.

And the further we get into this season (while acknowledging plenty can still change over the next several months), the more it looks like this might be the one Western Conference team with a serious shot to keep San Antonio out of the Finals.

Houston has a ferocious defense led by Amen Thompson. It has two players averaging over 20 points in Alperen Sengun and Kevin Durant. It has three more over 13 in Jabari Smith Jr., Thompson and Fred VanVleet. And it has another three over eight with Reed Sheppard, Tari Eason and Marcus Smart.

There's a good enough balance of scoring, experience level and size here to buy the Rockets as a very real threat to make a deep playoff run.

The Minnesota Timberwolves have more than adjusted to life without Anthony Edwards, and LaMelo Ball is a big reason why.

After going for 22 points and nine assists in 25 minutes on Thursday, Ball is now averaging 18.6 and 6.3 in 27.5 minutes, while shooting 40.6 percent from deep.

His playmaking is lifting his teammates. And surrounding him with their defense has helped him look—and play—far more committed on that end.

He and the Wolves have suddenly won five straight and have the best net rating in the league. And it's easy to imagine them as real contenders when Edwards returns.

Luka is averaging 38.6 points, and remarkably, may not be having quite as good a season as San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama.

After another undefeated week and a 10th straight victory, Wemby is now on pace for the highest single-season box plus/minus of all time. And his more basic numbers look legitimately Wilt-like.

In just 30.0 minutes per game, Wembanyama is putting up 30.3 points, 11.7 rebounds, 4.4 blocks, 2.8 assists and 1.2 steals. And his raw plus-minus of plus-225 leads the entire NBA.

This was a statement week for the Boston Celtics.

They went 4-0 and won all four of those games on the road. Two of the wins were over the Hornets and Bucks, but those victories came by an average of 29.5 points.

And most importantly, they went into Philadelphia and squashed the 76ers in Jaylen Brown's potential revenge game.

Brown and Philly will get other shots at the Celtics, but right now, replacing Brown with Paul George (a player better able to play a complementary role) and making Jayson Tatum the clear alpha looks like it was the right call.

articles.title: Kyrie Irving Trade Rumors Updated by NBA Insider with Latest Intel from 'Rival Teams'
articles.summary: Even though Kyrie Irving would seem less likely now to be moved before the NBA trade deadline in February with the Dallas Mavericks off to a strong start, that won't stop opposing clubs from at least kicking the tires to see if something can happen.
articles.body:
Even though Kyrie Irving would seem less likely now to be moved before the NBA trade deadline in February with the Dallas Mavericks off to a strong start, that won't stop opposing clubs from at least kicking the tires to see if something can happen.

Per The Athletic's Sam Amick , "rival teams" around the league still view Irving as someone who would generate significant trade interest because is the one potential target who can "truly change the playoff landscape" if a deal were to come together.

Any concerns about Irving's ability coming off a torn ACL that kept him out for the entire 2025-26 season have so far been alleviated. The 34-year-old is averaging 21.6 points per game on 47.9 percent shooting (39.0 percent from three) in 10 starts.

The Mavs have managed Irving's minutes so far this season. He is averaging 30.1 minutes per contest, which would be the fewest of his career if it stays at that level.

Despite the hiring of Masai Ujiri as team president in May, he has shown no inclination toward trading Irving. He said prior to the start of the season the organization "truly" believes in the nine-time All-Star and he can be part of what they want to build around Cooper Flagg.

The Flagg-Irving pairing has been working great so far. They have led the Mavs to a 7-5 record, including wins over the Oklahoma City Thunder and Houston Rockets.

Thursday's 133-94 loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves did pour some cold water on the Mavs' start.

Irving's contract situation also presents an interesting dilemma for Ujiri when thinking about the trade deadline. He has a $42.4 million player option for next season.

Assuming Irving remains healthy and continues to play well, it's reasonable to believe he would opt out for a multiyear deal. His age doesn't line up with the rebuilding timeline centered around Flagg, but the Mavs have plenty of financial wiggle room in the short-term because they don't have significant contracts on their books.

Flagg isn't eligible to sign an extension until the summer of 2028 and that deal wouldn't even kick in until the 2029-30 season. PJ Washington is currently Dallas' only player under contract with a guaranteed salary over $20 million in 2027-28.

Ujiri set this season up to be an evaluation period for this Mavs group. The early returns have been strong, but plenty of things can change between now and the Feb. 11 trade deadline that could make Irving a potential trade target.

Given the high number of injuries to star players that have already occurred this season, the Mavericks might be able to leverage those teams into securing a significant haul for Irving if they want to go in that direction.

articles.title: Jimmy Butler Pledges to Play for Warriors' NBA G League Affiliate During Knee Injury Rehab
articles.summary: Amid his recovery from a torn ACL, Jimmy Butler stated his desire this week to play a rehab game for the Golden State Warriors' G League affiliate, the Santa Cruz Warriors, before making his way back onto an NBA court.
articles.body:
Amid his recovery from a torn ACL, Jimmy Butler stated his desire this week to play a rehab game for the Golden State Warriors' G League affiliate, the Santa Cruz Warriors, before making his way back onto an NBA court.

Speaking to Nick Friedell of The Athletic, Butler said, "I'm going down to Santa Cruz to hoop. ... It may not be for long, but I'm going to play in Santa Cruz. I'm playing in a f--king game."

Butler's 2025-26 season was cut short when he tore his ACL in January, and although no official timeline for his return has been released by the Warriors, the 37-year-old veteran has grand plans in mind for his road to recovery.

When asked by Friedell if he has gotten clearance from Warriors general manager Mike Dunleavy to play in the G League, Butler said, "I don't got to clear s--t with nobody," before joking that he would "fistfight" Dunleavy to get his way.

Butler has the full support of Warriors head coach Steve Kerr regarding his plan to play a G League game, though.

"Oh, hell yeah," Kerr said. "I love that. Jimmy told you that? I love that. It's funny because I've always thought about that given my baseball fandom; you see these guys go to the minors all the time for a rehab stint and they get several games. It makes perfect sense, but I've never really seen a star player go to the G League. Has it happened?"

As noted by Friedell, no player of Butler's caliber has ever played a game in the G League before.

It is commonplace for rehabbing players to practice with G League teams before rejoining their NBA teams, but games are rarely part of the equation, particularly when it comes to star players.

Butler is a six-time All-Star, five-time All-NBA selection and five-time NBA All-Defensive Team selection.

Over 15 NBA seasons with the Chicago Bulls, Minnesota Timberwolves, Philadelphia 76ers, Miami Heat and Warriors, Butler boasts averages of 18.4 points, 5.4 rebounds, 4.4 assists and 1.6 steals per game.

He was trending toward a great 2025-26 season before tearing his ACL as well, averaging 20.0 points, 5.6 rebounds, 4.9 assists and 1.4 steals per contest.

Despite being without Butler, the Warriors are off to a great start this season, going 8-4, which places them sixth in the Western Conference.

articles.title: New NBA Trade Rumors Reveal Nets 'Will Listen' to Any Calls amid Julius Randle, MPJ Buzz
articles.summary: Having lost eight of 11 games to start the 2026-27 season, the Brooklyn Nets are keeping the door open to trade any of their veteran players on big contracts.
articles.body:
Having lost eight of 11 games to start the 2026-27 season, the Brooklyn Nets are keeping the door open to trade any of their veteran players on big contracts.

Per The Athletic's Sam Amick , the Nets "will listen" on any trade calls that come in with Julius Randle and Michael Porter Jr. being particularly attractive to playoff contenders looking for help.

Day'Ron Sharpe, Mo Wagner and Keon Ellis are among the other notable Nets players with no guaranteed money remaining on their contracts beyond this season.

Randle is still new to Brooklyn after being acquired as part of the four-team trade during the offseason that was headlined by LaMelo Ball going to the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Porter is in his second season with the Nets after being traded by the Denver Nuggets in the summer of 2025. The Nuggets included a 2032 first-round draft pick to sweeten the deal, which saw Cameron Johnson go back to Denver.

The Nets are well positioned with first-round draft picks in the future because they are also still owed three selections from the New York Knicks from the Mikal Bridges trade, but their current standing indicates they should keep adding more to the queue.

Brooklyn is only ahead of the Chicago Bulls and Milwaukee Bucks in the Eastern Conference standings.

Porter would also have value in a trade because he is on a $40.8 million expiring contract. The 28-year-old is averaging 21.5 points on 37.5 percent three-point shooting and 7.5 rebounds per game in 11 starts.

Randle's situation is a little more complicated because he holds a $35.8 million player option for next season, giving him some leverage over where he might end up.

A three-time All-Star, Randle has been remarkably consistent throughout his career. He is averaging 19.7 points, 6.5 rebounds and 5.0 assists per game in 2026-27. The 31-year-old has averaged at least 18 points, six rebounds and four assists per game in each of the past six seasons.

articles.title: Must-See 65: The plan to kill the NBA back-to-back and re-energize the sport's biggest stars
articles.summary: With injuries sweeping through the league's stars, it's time to move to a 65-game schedule.
articles.body:
It was well past midnight when the Philadelphia 76ers touched down in Charlotte. The star-studded team was in the middle of a back-to-back prepping for its league-high seventh game in just 12 days. You could call it an NBA "short night." Friday night in Philadelphia: a 7:30 p.m. ET national TV game against the defending champion New York Knicks. Shower, bus, shuffle onto the team plane for a nearly 500-mile trip down the coast. At the earliest, lights out at 2 a.m. ET. Then Saturday: an early 6 p.m. ET tip against the Hornets on Halloween.

Of the 426 back-to-backs on the NBA schedule, this was the second-shortest turnaround with travel: 22 1/2 hours, with an overnight flight in between.

Fans in Charlotte saw the cost. LeBron James and Joel Embiid jerseys filled the stands, but both James (sciatica) and Embiid (plantar fasciitis) were ruled out managing injuries on the second night of the back-to-back. Fans paid good money for tickets and TV packages, not to mention parking and concessions and merch, and expected to see them.

But don't blame the players. Blame the schedule.

In my decade-plus covering the NBA, I have written about back-to-backs many times before. But as the 76ers sideline reporter for NBC Sports Philadelphia this season, I hadn't experienced one quite like this. And it was only October. Hundreds more still litter the schedule. With injuries sweeping through the league's stars — Stephen Curry (oblique) is now out multiple weeks — and fan trust at stake, the fix is overdue:

Ban back-to-backs and move to a 65-game schedule.

The NBA has always sold its stars. Right now, the league is breaking that promise.

Anthony Edwards used to be a loud critic against load management. At his first All-Star appearance in 2023, the 21-year-old star responded to a question about the league's hot-button issue.

"Just play, man," Edwards said. "If you 80%, you gotta play. I don't like all the sitting, missing games stuff. These people might have enough money to come to one game. And that might be the game they come to and you sitting out."

Edwards walked the walk. Edwards played in nearly every game of that Timberwolves season, the first of three straight seasons playing 79 games. No All-Star played more than Edwards, per Stathead tracking, and the fans loved it.

Edwards was a box-office hit and seemed invincible, the face that could stem the tide of load management.

And then in March last season, his knee started barking. He looked limited against OKC in his 58th game and the medical team sidelined him. One pressing issue: He needed to play in seven of the 15 remaining games to qualify for postseason awards, which, until the OKC game, seemed easily attainable. His coach Chris Finch praised his Ironman courage and noted Edwards had played in 95% of his games in his career, "which is extremely rare."

But the game finally caught up to Edwards. He missed 11 of the team's next 14 games and hobbled through the worst postseason of his precocious career. He fell short of the 65 games needed for all-league awards and missed more time in the playoffs. The health problems have only continued. This season, after just four games, Edwards was shut down with issues in the same knee that he tried to play through last season. The team hopes he's back in two months after knee debridement surgery. This week, he was seen still on crutches. A league and its fans may wonder: Will he ever be the same?

Maybe Edwards saw this coming. The same week he was shut down, Adidas unveiled its latest commercial captioned "65 games one way or another" for its flagship player. The timing of its publication sliced like a knife. In the spot, Edwards, arguably the NBA's most marketable American star and once-crusader against load management, is seemingly surrendering to the reality of the 82-game grind. In the pre-taped ad, Edwards is holding auditions for his stand-in when he misses time. "If I gotta sit out this season, you gotta act like me, you gotta talk like me, most importantly you gotta hoop like me," Edwards cracked.

Edwards' body couldn't hold up and now his shoe company is mocking the whole thing. But it's no laughing matter for the players, fans and the league's business.

Edwards just one face of latest injury crisis

Injuries have dominated headlines in the early going. Less than 10 games into the season, Edwards was one of nine star players — as defined by the league's Player Participation Policy of having been named to at least one All-Star or All-NBA team in the previous three seasons — who have already suffered a significant injury. You can add Curry to this list.

The Oklahoma City Thunder, with dreams of being the league's next dynasty, have been decimated by the reality, with major injuries to stars Jalen Williams (broken fibula and dislocated ankle) and Chet Holmgren (knee), not to mention key player Cason Wallace, who is shelved indefinitely with a shoulder injury. Tyrese Haliburton, Jalen Duren and Kawhi Leonard are also injured on championship contenders.

The game is faster and more taxing than it was in previous generations. Steve Kerr told me during the 2025 playoffs that it's a young man's game, the sheer velocity making it tougher for vets in the playoffs. About a month after that, Haliburton tore his Achilles in Game 7 of the NBA Finals. Even the young players aren't immune to the harsh demands of the sport.

In 2023, when the NBA rolled out its Player Participation Policy, the NBA commissioned a 57-page study on load management. It didn't find evidence that load management affected injury rates in either direction. (Science is hard.) One chart, though, told a clear story that demands wholesale reform: The average star missed 10.4 games a season in the 1980s, growing gradually to 10.6 games a season in the 1990s, 13.9 in the 2000s and 17.4 in the 2010s. From 2019-20 through 2022-23, however, that number jumped to 23.9. Last season, I ran the numbers and it hit 27.7, more than two-and-a-half times the 1990s rate.

That's a lot of stars missing in action, and even more potential lifelong fans who are now looking elsewhere with their eyeballs and dollars. Fans waking up to find the news of another star getting hurt has become routine, even if, by my count, star injury rates are slightly down overall year over year. (Those Damian Lillard, Tyrese Haliburton, Kyrie Irving and Jayson Tatum DNPs last season added up quickly.) Even excluding last season's season-scrapping injuries, the overall trend line is unmistakable.

So, how do we get back to the pre-2000 DNP rates? Small tweaks haven't worked. A 40-minute game doesn't address the biggest problem: The sport is too taxing for so many games with crosscountry travel. A 65-game season that rejuvenates fan trust and interest is the answer. We need to invest and protect the stars that make the NBA what it is. We need to think about Felipe.

For the 76ers' back-to-back ending in Charlotte, what got me was seeing the kids in the stands, the ones who brought posters and chanted their favorite players' names only for the schedule to let them down.

This happens all too often. In 2023, an Argentinean boy named Felipe flew over 4,000 miles to see Jimmy Butler play in Miami. TNT cameras showed the devastation when the kid dropped his poster in shock when he learned Butler wasn't playing. Butler was a late scratch with lower back tightness. (Butler felt terrible and met with the family the next day with merch.)

The NBA has a real opportunity to further invest in delivering to families and younger fans who build core memories at games. Studies show that lifelong sports fandom is typically inherited by family ties and most were hooked by age 14 . The Felipe story went viral and he got taken care of, but I worry that most just go home and think twice about buying tickets next time, turning on their Nintendo Switch instead of the big game.

When I think about improving an already great league, a 65-game season that eliminates these zero-rest nights is key. Why am I targeting back-to-backs? The link to injuries is murky, but it's the clearest way to get stars on the floor, and that's what keeps fans coming back. I've shown that star players suit up for more than 90% of Cup games , higher than the regular-season norm. Part of that is the stakes, but part of it, I suspect, is the schedule-makers keeping Cup games off dreaded back-to-backs. In the playoffs, where there are no back-to-backs, stars don't sit for rest and play almost every game.

James and Embiid join a host of stars who have already missed the second night of a back-to-back this season. Curry, Luka Dončić, Paul George, Pascal Siakam and Kyrie Irving have all sat a zero-rest game in 2026-27. This season, stars have played in 73.5% of games on the second night of a back-to-back, compared with nearly 80% of all other games.

The product is also better without back-to-backs. Victor Wembanyama's Wilt impression last Wednesday — 52 points, 24 rebounds and 8 blocks — came on a day of rest. That's no fluke. Wembanyama is dunking 40% more when he isn't playing on the second night of a back-to-back, continuing last season's trend where, according to Stathead tracking, he dunked 25% more with at least one day of recovery. League-wide, dunks go up when players' bodies aren't run down on back-to-backs.

So with all that considered, here's my proposal.

Every team plays 65 games in the regular season. I'm calling it Must-See 65. The league and the players union agreed that 65 games makes a star's season count. Let's make it real with a 65-game schedule and let's make it must-see TV.

Say goodbye to the 82-game schedule and bring back appointment viewing. Continue to market the stars and deliver more on that promise. Restore trust among fans and make advertisers more confident with their investments.

The most common rebuttal is money: Critics claim that owners and players will never agree to give up that much revenue. But baseball's owners just proposed cutting eight games without cutting player salaries. Owners are warming up to the idea that fewer games can mean more valuable ones. NBA owners have a possible cushion, too: Each stands to collect a reported $650 million or more in upcoming expansion fees.

For players, the upside is health. Fewer games and no back-to-backs mean fewer nights playing banged up, and potentially longer careers, which can be worth millions in future earnings.

With expansion on the horizon, the time is now. Ten months ago, I campaigned for a 58-game schedule as part of Adam Silver's New Year's Resolutions. But with expansion imminent, I wasn't thinking big enough. Two more teams unlock a new billion-dollar revenue stream in my Must-See 65 proposal.

Let's get into it. Here are some key points of Must-See 65 that will help keep revenues neutral:

• With the expected expansion to Seattle and Las Vegas, the Emirates NBA Cup turns into a 32-team single-elimination tournament midseason, seeded by record. Capture some of the magical dust of March Madness, a tournament that reels in more than $1 billion a year. (Before expansion, the top two teams receive a bye.)

• This year, the Emirates NBA Cup Championship Game will be played at Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis. Double down on that. Break the 32 teams into four regional sites in cities that have dreams of having an NBA team: Nashville, Louisville, Kansas City and Mexico City. You want an NBA team? Show us. With lots of money and fans, of course.

• Some schedule housekeeping: In the regular season, play each team twice — one home, one away — for 60 non-Cup regular-season games. With Seattle and Las Vegas added, each team skips one game against two non-conference opponents on an eight-year rotation basis. The Cup will take care of the remaining five games, with makeup games at regional sites for those who are eliminated. (Before expansion, the NBA can add two regular-season games to reach 65. Maybe package a rivalry miniseries of three intradivision games?)

• Here's the best part: The winner of the 32-team tournament gets to decide their playoff opponent until the conference finals. Yes, that means if you win the NBA Cup, you're guaranteed a playoff spot. The Opponent Selection Show becomes a sponsored TV revenue driver.

Banning back-to-backs could be the NBA's version of the pitch clock in baseball: a fix that fans can feel immediately. Baseball's attendance has grown in three straight years since it was added and the fan base got younger. Packaged the right way, a new season format without back-to-backs could lead to a similar bump in eyeballs and youth engagement. No more need to wait until game day to see if the star is ruled out. No more sad Felipes.

Will fewer games raise ticket prices? Maybe. But tickets are already expensive and star absences can hurt the fan experience. Fans will pay more for Hamilton tickets if Lin-Manuel Miranda is on the bill and they have a better chance of leaving happy.

The sleep-deprived Halloween game was notable for another reason. Fans in Charlotte saw a shorthanded Sixers team stumble its way through the game, eking out a victory in the closing minutes. Jaylen Brown was the only Sixer to dunk in the game.

Two days later, with a day off, the Sixers' star-studded lineup of Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe, Brown, James and Embiid returned to the floor. With more recovery for its stars, the team put on a show in a home win against the Bulls. The dunk count that night? Nine. That's the NBA that fans pay to see.

articles.title: Joel Embiid Gets Encouraging Message from VJ Edgecombe amid 76ers Star's Sluggish Start
articles.summary: With Joel Embiid off to a slow start for the Philadelphia 76ers, VJ Edgecombe has offered words of encouragement to the seven-time All-Star.
articles.body:
With Joel Embiid off to a slow start for the Philadelphia 76ers, VJ Edgecombe has offered words of encouragement to the seven-time All-Star.

Following the Sixers' 123-112 win over the Toronto Raptors on Thursday, Edgecombe told reporters he has said to Embiid that "nobody can stop you" on the court and you can see him "starting to find his rhythm."

"I just try to tell him all the time, 'Bro, you were MVP of the league,'" Edgecombe added.

Embiid put up 20 points against the Raptors, his first time hitting that mark since Nov. 4. He only shot 7-of-17 from the field, marking his ninth time making under 50 percent of his attempts in 11 starts.

The 32-year-old is on pace to set career-lows in points per game (17.9), field-goal percentage (37.4) and three-point percentage (11.1).

Despite Embiid's struggles thus far, the 76ers have been able to win games. They improved to 10-3 after beating Toronto. Only the Boston Celtics (10-2) have a better record among Eastern Conference teams.

articles.title: Doug McDermott Retires After 12 NBA Seasons with Bulls, Knicks, Thunder, Spurs, More
articles.summary: Former first-round draft pick Doug McDermott has retired after 12 seasons in the NBA.
articles.body:
Former first-round draft pick Doug McDermott has retired after 12 seasons in the NBA.

McDermott's agent, Mark Bartelstein of Priority Sports, issued a statement announcing his client's decision.

McDermott put himself on the national radar during his four years at Creighton from 2010 to 2014. He led the Bluejays to three consecutive NCAA tournament appearances over his final three years.

Creighton won at least 23 games in each of his four seasons. McDermott was an All-American first-team selection in three consecutive years. He led the nation in scoring average with 26.7 points per game as a senior to earn consensus National Player of the Year honors.

The Bluejays retired McDermott's No. 3 jersey in December 2023.

McDermott parlayed his college success into becoming the No. 11 pick by the Denver Nuggets in the 2014 NBA draft. His rights were traded to the Chicago Bulls, where he spent the first two-plus years of his career.

The Bulls traded McDermott to the Oklahoma City Thunder midway through the 2016-17 season. He bounced around the league from that point on, including stints with the New York Knicks, Dallas Mavericks, Indiana Pacers, San Antonio Spurs and Sacramento Kings.

McDermott finished his career with the Kings during the 2025-26 season. He appeared in 29 games off the bench, with his final appearance coming on April 12.

In 726 career NBA games, McDermott averaged 8.5 points and 2.1 rebounds per contest. His 41.0 percent success rate from three-point range ranks 22nd all-time.

articles.title: Jalen Green Eyed as Trade Candidate in New NBA Rumors amid Suns' Early-Season Struggles
articles.summary: Amid a 5-6 start to the season, the Phoenix Suns could look to shake things up in an effort to turn things around with Jalen Green's future in the desert a hot topic of discussion throughout the NBA.
articles.body:
Amid a 5-6 start to the season, the Phoenix Suns could look to shake things up in an effort to turn things around with Jalen Green's future in the desert a hot topic of discussion throughout the NBA.

Per The Athletic's Sam Amick , the belief from opposing clubs is the Suns are "motivated" to trade Green for a proven point guard who can run the offense for head coach Jordan Ott.

Amick cited one person with the Suns as insisting they will "remain patient" with their roster and don't plan to engage in any serious trade discussions until later in the season.

Green was acquired by the Suns from the Houston Rockets in the Kevin Durant trade with the hope he could develop into a strong second option next to Devin Booker.

The No. 2 pick in the 2021 NBA draft, Green was only 23 at the time of the trade and averaged 21.0 points during the 2024-25 season with the Rockets. Hamstring and knee injuries limited him to just 32 games in his first year with Phoenix.

Green has started all 11 games the Suns have played so far this season, but his output is way down. He is averaging a career-low 11.8 points per game on 41.9 percent shooting (27.0 percent from three).

It's unclear how much interest there would be in Green if he were made available due to his contract. The 24-year-old is making $36.2 million this season and holds a $36 million player option for 2027-28.

Scoring efficiency has never been a strength of Green's game. His best field-goal percentage was 42.6 percent as a rookie and he has only shot better at 35 percent from three once (35.4 in 2024-25).

The Suns have the 12th-worst net rating in the NBA right now. One encouraging sign is they have won four of their last five games, including a victory over the Rockets on Nov. 7.

articles.title: Defense team tries to tie NBA champion Chris Bosh to Palisades arsonist case, citing firework evidence: report
articles.summary: The defense team for Jonathan Rinderknecht is seeking testimony about a firework that allegedly launched from NBA champion Chris Bosh's property.
articles.body: NBA legend Chris Bosh has been drawn into the Palisades arson case. The defense team for Jonathan Rinderknecht is seeking testimony about a firework that allegedly launched from Bosh's property on Jan. 1, 2025, the night the Lachman Fire ignited. articles.title: How real are the Lakers, Spurs and the 10 teams slugging it out in the West?
articles.summary: Breaking down the early-season runs from a loaded Western Conference.
articles.body:
The Western Conference is tough, a slugfest, a large predicament. None of that is new information. There was, however, a stat from last week that stopped me in my tracks. It was the moment where the West's top-five teams were all on winning streaks of at least four games for the first time since conferences began.

All of the current top 10 teams in the West have won at least six of their past 10 games. All of the current top-five are on a winning streak. Six of the current top-10 teams have won their last game. The four teams that have lost? It's because they had to play another top Western Conference team.

According to the NBA, eight of the top-10 teams in offensive rating are in the West, six of the top-10 teams in defensive rating are in the West, and seven of the top-10 teams in net rating are in the West.

It is still early in the process of the regular season. These teams are still learning who they are on this journey. It is also very real that early success can lead to even more buy-in, which can sustain a team over the course of a season. How real are these early-season runs from the Western Conference? Let's take a look at each team.

Yes, Luka Dončić is still on a preposterous run to start the season. Yes, Austin Reaves (who suffered a heel injury on Wednesday) is having a career. And, yes, the Lakers currently have the best offense in basketball. What could make this stick, though, is the belief this team has and the effort it's given on defense.

There is an activity the Lakers have brought to the defensive end of the floor. It's not particularly new from what they've attempted to do in the past, but the execution appears more consistent throughout the roster. Switching on- and off-ball actions, working to contain drives and showing early help have been hallmarks of the Lakers' defense.

Walker Kessler's impact has been felt with his work to not just protect the rim, but to consistently rotate to get in position. There's a reason he leads the league in total contested shots (150, 11.5 per game). Whether it's from the baseline, elbow or wing, Kessler's timing has been key in the Lakers' ability to protect the paint (opponents average 43.1 points in the paint, fourth-lowest in league).

When the Lakers trend smaller with Kessler off the court, the switching becomes more constant and the attempts at activity ramp up, with multiple lineups that can consistently hit those notes. They'll be tested by switching on both ends eventually, but it feels like the vision and the formula are in alignment.

If there were any questions about the Spurs' ability to rise back to the top of the Western Conference after a wobbly 0-2 start … I believe 10 straight wins provides an answer. The shift to the three-guard lineup of De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper has had its bumpy moments, but appears to be turning a corner.

We are starting to feel the moments where a defense is in rotation and all three can attack. That shift also does not take away from the fact the Spurs still can have 48 minutes of quality guard play throughout a game. This opens up lineup versatility (which will be huge come playoff time) and has contributed to the Spurs' overall offensive balance.

It also helps that Victor Wembanyama has gotten even better on both ends. In his last five games, he's averaging 36.6 points, 13 rebounds, and 5 blocks in 28.4 minutes a night, while shooting 65.6% from the field and 41.4% from 3. His physicality is showing up in different ways: working to catch in his spots; being in position to set screens lower on the floor; releasing to his rolls quicker. It'll be hard to doubt the Spurs if the execution continues to level up.

Minnesota had shown the formula and potency of its starting lineup to start this season. That the Timberwolves have been able to expand it while Anthony Edwards has been on the shelf speaks volumes. If the question is where exactly would LaMelo Ball elevate the Wolves, the answer has been everywhere.

Ball's playmaking has enhanced their transition and pick-and-roll attack. The shotmaking and drives have added another layer. Jonathan Kuminga has continued to showcase the value of being wanted by doing exactly what the Wolves have needed him to do. Jaden McDaniels and Ayo Dosunmu remain aggressive. What boosts this attack is the fact that the strong defense has held up: activity, ball pressure, off-ball stunts to disrupt. Size and length to switch and bother with Rudy Gobert roaming in the paint can cause chaos. It's hard to imagine this team will not continue to build on its emerging confidence and chemistry.

It's the combination of a reliable, strong defense and a commitment to evolving their offense that has helped the Rockets ascend to start this season. Their best moments have come when they have gotten the ball up quick, gotten to multiple actions and kept things moving.

Kevin Durant is fully scoring within the flow of their offense, meaning you have to defend multiple things and then Kevin Durant gets the ball. Fred VanVleet has steadied the ship, mixing in pull-up 3s while reading defenses to make plays (without turning the ball over). It's not just that all of their young players are able to "slide down a slot" — their roles are more concise, allowing for more consistency and confidence. The challenge is, will they revert to old habits if either the defense or offense slides backward?

A hallmark of this Blazers start has been a collective commitment to buying into their roles and working to do the little things every single night. Damian Lillard's return has been riddled of reminders of the talent he brings to the table. The logo 3s are one thing, the ability to mix in a timely drive is another, and he's willing to put the work in on the defensive end.

Toumani Camara will attempt to guard everyone in an opposing jersey. The emergence of Sidy Cissoko means the Blazers have a consistency of guard, wing and big play throughout their lineups. It's less about if they can do it, more of a matter of how many times can they repeat it. No matter where they land in the standings, you'll have to deal with the Blazers all year long. Will they be ready for the success that comes with it?

Well, the test for Golden State now is how real can this run be with Stephen Curry out for an extended amount of time? Curry was tremendous to start the season, but the Warriors were combining his excellent play with working to evolve offensively. More pick-and-roll (with more cutting around it), more willingness to attack matchups, mixing in their traditional splits vs. leaning on it as a base.

Yaxel Lenderborg has been a revelation, continuing to gain trust with each performance. Now we'll see just how strong that base is and if the defense that has impressed early can hold up in a scenario where they will have to get stops. It's always been about if the Warriors can win enough regular-season games to get the true payoff in the playoffs.

An unfortunate amount of injuries has led to the Thunder having to work through a different kind of adversity early in the season. If there is one thing about this team, it's that it's always believed in internal growth and optionality. The Thunder have always worked to stay consistent with their approach, and that's what may be the thing that helps lift them through this season.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander being moved off-ball can make him more sudden in a universe where teams may throw more attention his way. There's plenty of opportunity for Jared McCain and Ajay Mitchell to make an impact offensively. But can they grind out enough offense over the course of the season? If nothing else this team will have to defend at an elite level, and if the defense sticks, the Thunder will be no fun to deal with.

What a contrast of two months as the Grizzlies went 6-0 in October and have gone 1-4 as of this writing in November. And all four of those losses came in the Grindhouse; home losses are the most consistent regret a Western Conference team can have.

There's a reason for their early success, though: It's been a team effort on both ends. Cameron Boozer has helped to elevate what they want to get to offensively. Ty Jerome has been game to take, make, decel and stepback his way to victory. There's a sneaky depth to this team that can be felt from game to game. The big thing is seeing how they adjust as more scouting reports and game plans come in. Taking the league by surprise is one thing, but how will they respond once they've earned a level of respect?

This is not the start the Nuggets had in mind, but the building blocks have not disappeared. On the season, Jamal Murray is averaging 26.2 points on 50.9% shooting from the field and 51.3% from 3. Nikola Jokić is still Nikola Jokić despite feelings he has fallen off. Cam Johnson has stayed aggressive, DeMar DeRozan adds a different element. The lineup versatility unlocked by the play of Spencer Jones and Trevon Brazile should pay off down the line.

The biggest question is, can they get enough out of their defense and can their offense still deliver the fastball? We know how tough Jokić/Murray/Aaron Gordon can be to defend, but if opponents find a consistent comfort, how much does that change the Nuggets' winning formula?

Cooper Flagg's start to the season is going to bring him and this Mavericks team into conversations that may not have been expected this soon. The team's build is what has intrigued me. Improving on both ends of the floor is not easy, and Dallas has risen from 27th in offensive rating and 19th in defensive rating last season to 12th in offensive rating and ninth in defensive rating. That is something.

Dusty May has built in principles the Mavericks have worked to hit. An offense that enhances what Flagg brings to the table, takes nothing away from Kyrie Irving and also empowers the rest of the roster is a positive. Defensively, they have several lineups that can have a lot of size and switchability, and they tend to be a bend-don't-break type of team at their peak. Drives are hard to come by, shots are contested in the paint, you just have to deal with them. As the season progresses, they will have to navigate learning how to win and finding a way to do what they do well consistently.

articles.title: Brett Yormark has a new home in Milan
articles.summary: The outgoing Big 12 commissioner will lead Milan Sports & Entertainment, a new holding company backed by RedBird Capital Partners.
articles.body:
Brett Yormark's next move is taking him well outside the Big 12 footprint.

The outgoing Big 12 commissioner is heading to Milan, Italy, where he has been named chief executive of Milan Sports & Entertainment, a newly launched holding company backed by RedBird Capital Partners , the investment firm behind Italian soccer powerhouse AC Milan.

Yormark's new job will be about much more than soccer.

MSE will bring together RedBird's investments in sports, business and live entertainment in Milan, with Yormark overseeing the company's business strategy and efforts to expand its presence internationally.

"It's an honor and a privilege to take on this role in a city with Milan's history and passion for sport," Yormark said in the announcement . "I understand the responsibility that comes with leading an organization connected to institutions that mean so much to their supporters and communities. Throughout my career, I have helped sports organizations evolve, expand their reach and create new opportunities, and I look forward to drawing on that experience to execute RedBird's vision for MSE."

One of the biggest projects on his plate will be the development of a new 71,500-seat stadium for AC Milan and city rival Inter Milan. The two clubs are working together on the venue, which will replace the historic San Siro stadium.

But RedBird has bigger ambitions for the city.

The company also plans to explore building a venue-management business focused on food and beverage, merchandise and premium hospitality. It is also evaluating the possibility of acquiring a Milan franchise in the proposed NBA Europe league , developing another sports and entertainment venue in nearby San Donato Milanese and expanding the city's presence in international tennis.

Yormark will report directly to RedBird founder and managing partner Gerry Cardinale. His new role is expected to begin after his departure from the Big 12.

That departure was announced at the end of October, bringing an end to a four-year run as commissioner of the conference. Yormark, who took over in 2022, oversaw the additions of eight schools, including BYU and Utah, while helping guide the league through major changes in college athletics.

BYU had been invited to join the league just before Yormark assumed his position.

Under his leadership, the Big 12 secured its latest media rights agreement, which pays member schools more than $30 million annually. The conference also saw significant growth in sponsorship and partnership revenue.

Yormark is expected to remain with the Big 12 through the end of January, giving the conference time to find its next commissioner.

Now, after spending the last several years navigating the changing landscape of college athletics, Yormark is preparing for a new challenge: helping build Milan into an even bigger international sports and entertainment destination.

articles.title: Guerschon Yabusele claimed his Greek team could beat 'quite a few' in NBA
articles.summary: During a recent interview, former NBA player Guerschon Yabusele made a bold claim about Panathinaikos in the Greek Basketball League and EuroLeague.
articles.body:
During a recent interview, former NBA player Guerschon Yabusele made a bold claim about Panathinaikos in the Greek Basketball League and EuroLeague.

Yabusele, selected No. 16 overall in the 2026 NBA Draft, played for the Boston Celtics and in the NBA G League before eventually heading overseas to continue his basketball career. After enjoying stints in China as well as France and Spain, the big man was a breakout star during the 2024 Olympics.

He signed to play the 2024-25 campaign with the Philadelphia 76ers, then played with the New York Knicks and Chicago Bulls in 2025-26. This summer, he signed with Panathinaikos B.C. in Athens. The 40-time Greek League champions, who have also won the EuroLeague seven times including most recently in 2024, is considered one of the stronger international clubs.

According to Yabusele, however, the team is so strong that he recently said he feels they could beat "quite a few" teams in the NBA.

Among those on the roster with Yabusele include other former NBA players including Kendrick Nunn, Isaac Bonga, Juancho Hernangomez, and Nigel Hayes-Davis. International stars like Sylvain Francisco and Mathias Lessort play crucial roles for the team as well.

Panathinaikos currently sits atop the EuroLeague standings with an 8-2 record so far this season. While they may seem like a bunch of NBA outcasts, there is also an undeniable synergy that comes with this level of success.

Sure, we know what Yabusele looked like in a smaller role playing in the United States. But with a higher usage rate overseas, he is a much different player who can make a far bigger impact.

As of right now, questions like these are purely hypothetical. But one day, as NBA commissioner Adam Silver pushes harder for the launch of NBA Europe , we may actually get a more serious answer to these type of questions.

Eventually, one proposed goal of NBA Europe is to integrate international teams into the in-season tournament NBA Cup ( via CBS Sports ):

"We have something we call the NBA Cup, a midseason tournament ... You could imagine teams from Europe, potentially Africa, competing in that tournament. You possibly could see teams coming into our playoffs, top seeds from other leagues."

That isn't exactly on the immediate horizon for Yabusele to prove his point on this current roster, of course.

But in the future, it would be fascinating to see how a team of veterans like Panathinaikos would fare against a rebuilding squad like the Milwaukee Bucks.

articles.title: New NBA Trade Rumors on Magic's Anthony Black After Contract Extension Talks Fizzled Out
articles.summary: Orlando Magic guard Anthony Black could be on the move before the NBA's trade deadline in February, The Athletic's Sam Amick reported.
articles.body:
Orlando Magic guard Anthony Black could be on the move before the NBA's trade deadline in February, The Athletic's Sam Amick reported.

According to Spotrac , the Magic are just $2.5 million below the second apron threshold, which could make it difficult for the team to sign Black to a long-term contract. The 22-year-old was unable to reach an agreement with the Magic for an extension this summer, and he is on track to be a restricted free agent after this season.

That dynamic has rival executives wondering if Black "might eventually be available," but team and league sources with knowledge of the Magic's thinking "pushed back" on the notion of Black being traded, according to Amick.

It makes sense for the Magic to keep the focus off of potential trade buzz as they look to get their season back on track. Orlando stumbled out of the gate and opened the 2026-27 season with a 4-7 record.

Orlando already has significant contracts on its books. Franz Wagner, Paolo Banchero, Desmond Bane and Jalen Suggs are all signed to long-term deals that are worth over $30 million annually. Those deals could complicate any sizable commitment to Black.

If Orlando becomes one of the teams looking to trade away players in exchange for draft capital, Black would likely be one of the top candidates.

articles.title: Are De’Aaron Fox, Devin Vassell playing tonight? Spurs vs. Warriors injury report
articles.summary: The San Antonio Spurs could be without two key contributors for Friday night’s NBA Cup matchup against the Golden State Warriors, as guards De’Aaron Fox and...
articles.body:
The San Antonio Spurs could be without two key contributors for Friday night's NBA Cup matchup against the Golden State Warriors , as guards De'Aaron Fox and Devin Vassell received injury updates.

San Antonio's latest injury report lists Fox as questionable with left hip soreness and Vassell as questionable with left adductor tightness.

The Spurs (10-2) will host the Warriors (8-4) at 9:30 p.m. ET on Prime Video, looking to extend their winning streak to 11 games after overcoming an 0-2 start.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Both players' availability remains uncertain ahead of the contest, with San Antonio attempting to maintain its early-season momentum.

Fox last appeared in San Antonio's 124-119 victory over the Chicago Bulls on Wednesday, finishing with 17 points, nine assists, four rebounds and three steals in 31 minutes.

The veteran guard shot 7-for-17 from the field and 2-for-7 from 3-point range, helping San Antonio complete a four-game road trip undefeated.

Meanwhile, Vassell missed Wednesday's victory because of his adductor injury, marking his second consecutive absence. His questionable designation leaves open the possibility of returning against Golden State.

Fox is averaging 14.2 points, 6.2 assists and 4.3 rebounds through 12 games this season while shooting 51.4% from the field.

Vassell has averaged 11.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 3.1 assists through 10 appearances, shooting 35.6% from beyond the arc.

The 26-year-old last appeared in San Antonio's 125-103 victory over the Portland Trail Blazers on Nov. 7, recording 15 points, three assists, two rebounds and two steals in 21 minutes.

Spurs, Warriors dealing with injuries ahead of NBA Cup clash

San Antonio's injury report also lists veteran forward Tobias Harris as out with a left calf strain and rookie Jayden Quaintance as out following right knee surgery.

Meanwhile, Golden State will be without Stephen Curry, who suffered a right oblique tear during Wednesday's 115-108 loss to the Houston Rockets and is expected to miss at least two weeks.

The Warriors' injury report also lists Jimmy Butler III, Moses Moody, and Brandon Williams as out.

Despite their injury concerns, the Spurs enter Friday's matchup riding a 10-game winning streak, with their latest victory featuring 32 points, nine rebounds and five blocks from Victor Wembanyama.

San Antonio will look to maintain its momentum against a Golden State team attempting to rebound from Wednesday's loss without its star guard.
